newsitem.title: USA: Clinton encouraged by Kremlin change before summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton encouraged by Kremlin change before summit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton left Washington on Wednesday night for a summit in Finland with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, expressing optimism about the Russian leader's latest Kremlin changes.
"I'm encouraged by the new economic theme President Yeltsin announced this week," Clinton said shortly before he left for Helsinki. "It underscores Russia's commitment to continued reform."

Yeltsin in recent days has shaken up his Cabinet in a move intended, at least in part, to re-establish his authority after long illness and to bring market-oriented economic reformers into senior Cabinet positions.

Anatoly Chubais, a prominent reformer recently restored to power as a first deputy premier, said on Tuesday the radical reshuffle was not yet over. "There will be more surprises," he told commercial NTV television.

"Now, the challenge is to create a climate that actually attracts more investment and promotes more trade so that Russia will have real economic growth," said Clinton, adding that he and Yeltsin "will discuss the steps that both of us will take to create that climate."
Clinton met with senior advisers to study the implications of the changes before making his remarks to reporters at the White House.

The wheelchair-bound Clinton, who underwent knee surgery last Friday to reattach a torn tendon suffered when he stumbled on some stairs, arrived at Andrews Air Force Base in a specially equipped white van.
The president, preceeded by his doctor carrying a set of crutches, was rolled onto a platform elevator and lifted aboard Air Force One for the overnight flight to Helsinki.
The Finland summit was expected to focus on Russia's opposition to NATO plans to expand its membership to include some of Moscow's onetime Warsaw Pact allies.

The president crammed his last few hours of White House time with domestic politics, trying to break an impasse in talks with Republican congressional leaders on balancing the federal budget. Clinton also had more physical therapy for his injured right knee.
The Helsinki meeting marks the first personal encounter for the U.S. and Russian presidents since an April summit in Moscow.

Ironically, the Finnish city replaced Washington, the venue originally scheduled, in order to make the trip less arduous for Yeltsin, who had heart by-pass surgery late last year and has struggled with double pneumonia more recently.

Senior administration officials stress that they expect no dramatic breakthroughs at the summit. Instead, they hope for progress in smoothing over divisive issues like the prospective NATO expansion and perhaps making some progress toward a charter spelling out NATO-Russia relations.
Washington also hopes to begin a new round of talks on nuclear missile reductions with Moscow, but first wants the Russian parliament to ratify the long-delayed START-2 treaty, signed in 1993.
